pageTexts: JEM 53 Journal of Emergency Management  Vol. 21, No. 1, January/February 2023 Current flood warning system in Japan and its effectiveness  in mobilizing evacuation: Lessons from case studies Guangwei Huang, PhD Juan Fan  ABSTRACT An  effective  flood  warning  system  is  crucial  for   successful  flood  management.  Flood  warning  systems   have  been  developed  in  many  countries  across  the   world.  However,  scientific  literature  on  flood  warning   systems has been mainly focused on technical capacity  building,  and  the  effectiveness  of  warning  systems  in   mobilizing evacuation was much understudied. Japan  is  a  country  with  a  long  history  of  fighting  against   flood disasters; the evaluation of its practices in provid- ing  flood  warnings  and  the  effectiveness  are  certainly   important  for  further  flood  research  development  in   Japan, and sharing the experience and lessons with the  rest of the world will contribute to flood damage reduc- tion  on  a  global  scale.  Following  this  line  of  thinking,   this  article  is  intended  to  present  a  clear  and  concise   picture of the current flood warning system in Japan,  which has been poorly documented up until now. It is  also aimed at providing a performance assessment for  the flood warning system through case study approach  and  the  use  of  Strengths,  Weaknesses,  Opportunities,   and  Threats  (SWOT)  model.  Through  analyses,  the   pros  and  cons  of  the  current  flood  warning  system  in   Japan  are  highlighted,  and  the  directions  for  further   development and refinement are explained. Key  words:  flood  warning,  evacuation,  Chikuma   River, Kuma River, SWOT INTRODUCTION Flood warning systems are a crucial component of  flood disaster management because they can save lives  and reduce damage to individual property and social  infrastructure. As the population living in flood-prone  areas and the value of urban and rural assets exposed  to flood risk are growing rapidly due to urbanization  and climate change, a better and effective flood early  warning  system  is  in  high  demand.  Having  such  a   system enables authorities to take appropriate action  such as evacuation instruction and dam or retarding  basin operation in advance of a flood event to avoid or  minimize catastrophic outcomes when severe weather  strikes. In contrast to flood forecasting systems, which  assess flood risk, the main purpose of a warning sys- tem is to issue warnings when a flood is approaching,  imminent,  or  already  becoming  a  disaster.  Moreover,   the  multifunctionality  of  flood  warning  systems  can   also  promote  and  improve  community  preparedness   for  flood  disasters  and  increase  understanding  of   risks  and  appropriate  flood  responses.  Because  of  its   importance,  flood  warning  systems  have  been  estab- lished in many places across the world. 1-3  According to  a study by Perera, 4  the number of flood early warning  systems  nearly  doubled  since  2000.  Although  many   research  works  on  flood  warning  systems  have  been   conducted  from  various  perspectives  during  the  last   two  decades,  these  studies  were  either  conducted   for  technology  development 5-9   or  information  dis- semination-centered  and  community-focused, 10-12   the   actual  operation  of  flood  warning  system  in  warning   issuance  and  its  effectiveness  in  mobilizing  evacua- tion have been very much understudied. The current  increase in the number and degree of flood disasters  makes the further development or refinement of flood  warning systems a necessity for establishing a society  resilient  to  climate  change. 54 Journal of Emergency Management  Vol. 21, No. 1, January/February 2023 assessment of the effectiveness of the system in issu- ing warnings and mobilizing residents for evacuation  through case study approach. The value of this paper  is to promote communication about the need to inte- grate river engineering with social characteristics for  better flood emergency management. MATERIALS AND METHODS This study employed a mixed methods approach.  First,  it  used  document  analysis  to  synthesize  tech- nical  details  for  clarifying  the  state  of  the  art  in   flood warning and emergency management in Japan.  Document  analysis  is  a  form  of  qualitative  research   in which documents are interpreted by the researcher  to  give  voice  and  meaning  around  an  assessment   topic, 13   and  often  used  in  combination  with  other   research methods as a means of triangulation. Target  documents  of  this  study  are  technical  reports  of  the   Ministry  of  Land,  Infra-structure,  Transport  and   Tourism  (MLIT),  and  Prefectural  and  Municipality   Governments  of  Japan.  Second,  after  revealing  tech- nical  details  of  the  flood  warning  system  in  Japan,   this  work  used  case  study  approach  to  evaluate  the   overall  performance  of  the  current  flood  warning   system  in  Japan  and  to  gain  a  better  understanding   of  the  direction  for  further  development  of  the  flood   warning system. Two cases were chosen in this study. The  first  is  the  flooding  in  the  middle  reaches   of  the  Chikuma  River  in  2019,  which  caused  seri- ous  damage  in  the  Nagano  Prefecture. 14   Chikuma   River  is  the  longest  and  widest  river  in  Japan,  flow- ing  through  three  prefectures:  Nagano,  Gunma,  and   Niigata.  As  it  runs  from  the  Nagano  Prefecture  into   the  Niigata  Prefecture,  the  waterway  is  renamed  to   the Shinano River, and it finally empties into the Sea  of  Japan.  Historical  records  showed  that  26  large- scale  flood  disasters  have  occurred  in  the  watershed   of  the  Chikuma  River  from  1742  to  2020,  and  11  of   them occurred since 1980. 15  In 2019, the levee of the  waterway  at  the  Hoyasu  location  breached,  and  the   inundation resulted in a 974,000,000 JPY loss in the  Nagano City. 16  There is a hydrological gauging station  (Kuiseke) 25.6 km upstream of the levee breach site,  and  another  one  (Tategahana)  5.5  m  downstream  of   the breaching site. Water level monitoring data from  2010 to 2019 from the two stations were analyzed to  examine the appropriateness of the warnings issued.  This study also collected various information related  to  evacuation,  interviewed  11  local  residents  in  the   most  damaged  area,  and  conducted  a  questionnaire   survey  to  identify  problems  in  emergency  manage- ment  with  a  particular  focus  on  emergency  informa- tion dissemination among foreigners living in Nagano  City. The rationale is that it is important to evaluate  a flood warning system from both hardware (technical  details) and software (convincing people to evacuate). The  main  questions  in  the  questionnaire  survey   for  non-Japanese  residents  were:  (1)  do  you  speak   Japanese,  (2)  did  you  receive  emergency  information   and  from  where,  and  (3)  did  you  evacuate  following   emergency calls. For Japanese residents, the questions  were:  (1)  did  you  receive  emergency  information  and   from where, (2) did you evacuate following emergency  calls,  (3)  if  yes,  the  evacuation  was  carried  out  by  a   car or on foot, and (4) if not, what are the reasons. The  interview probed into the flood risk perception of resi- dents and asked about their experience in the evacua- tion process and opinions on emergency management. The  second  is  the  flooding  of  the  Kuma  River  in   2020, which caused serious damage in Hitoyoshi City,  Nagano  Prefecture.  The  Kuma  River  is  the  longest   river  in  the  Kyushu  region  of  Japan  and  known  as   one  of  the  three  most  rapid  rivers  of  Japan.  Eleven   major flood disasters occurred in the watershed since  1927  according  to  the  Kyushu  Disaster  Database. 17   In  2020,  a  torrential  rain  caused  levee  breaches  and   overflows at multiple locations in Hitoyoshi City. The  flood  disaster  claimed  several  dozens  of  lives  and   inundated 7,400 houses. 18  There are two hydrological  gauging stations in the most affected area, so that the  water level data of the two stations were analyzed to  evaluate the warning system in this river. It also col- lected  various  information  related  to  evacuation  and   conducted  questionnaire  survey  for  problem  identifi- cation like the first case. For  the  two  cases,  field  inspections  were  con- ducted  at  locations  where  levee  breach  occurred,   and  questionnaire  surveys  were  carried  out  in  both   Nagano  City  and  Hitoyoshi  City  for  further  problem   identification. Finally,  by  combining  document  analysis  results   and  findings  from  hydrological  data  analysis  and   questionnaire  survey,  both  pros  and  cons  of  the  cur - rent  flood  warning  system  of  Japan  were  assessed,   and  a  new  framework  for  flood  emergency  response   was  developed  based  on  a  Strengths,  Weaknesses,   Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) cross analysis. The research methodology of the present study is  illustrated in  Figure  1. Such a hybrid approach leads  to  a  complete  picture  of  the  system  with  technical   details  and  provides  an  assessment  of  the  effective- ness  of  the  system  through  case  study.  Furthermore,   it aims at more than case study, attempting to gener - alize using framework analysis. RESULTS Flood warning system in Japan Document  analysis  revealed  that  Japan  has  a   five-stage  flood  warning  system  at  present,  which   is  based  on  information  on  heavy  rainfall  from  the   Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) and hydrological  monitoring stations. 19  It provides municipalities with  criteria  to  issue  emergency  response  instruction  of   different level. The structural details are compiled in  Table  1, which are little known to scientific communi- ties outside of Japan. In the system, Level 1 is an early warning issued  by  the  JMA  for  the  possibility  of  heavy  rain.  Level   2  warning  is  also  issued  by  the  JMA  for  heavy  rain   and  flooding  alert.  Level  3  indicates  that  danger  is   approaching,  and  the  warning  is  issued  by  munici- palities. At this stage, the elderly and disabled should  start evacuation, while others prepare for evacuation.  Level 4 indicates the need for a full evacuation. Level  5  signifies  the  occurrence  of  disaster  and  the  need  to   take  whatever  action  is  necessary  to  safeguard  one’s   own  life.  In  implementing  this  system,  a  technical   question is how to determine each level. Currently, the  criterion is the river water level. 20  Each warning level  is  associated  with  a  water  level  in  the  river  channel.   Particularly  important  are  the  so-called  evacuation   judgment water level and the flood danger water level.  Once evacuation judgment water level is reached, local  government should issue evacuation instruction to the  elderly and disabled. As water level rises from evacua- tion judgment water level to flood danger water level,  evacuation  instruction  will  be  issued  to  all  in  risky   areas.  In  theory,  the  determination  of  the  two  water   levels  should  be  based  on  records  of  the  water  level   rising  rate  at  the  gauging  site  to  provide  sufficient   lead time to all, especially the elderly and disabled to  prepare  for  evacuation.  However,  the  actual  setting   of  evacuation  judgment  water  level  and  flood  danger   water  level  has  not  been  well  documented,  and  its   effectiveness  in  mobilizing  evacuation  has  not  been   evaluated so far. According  to  the  Basic  Act  on  Disaster  Manage- ment  of  Japan  established  in  1961,  municipalities   can  direct  residents  for  evacuation  in  the  case  of   emergency and are responsible for preparing regional  Disaster Prevention Plans, which includes criteria for  issuance  of  evacuation  information,  and  implement- ing it as well. In the past, two kinds of warning could  be issued at Level 4, namely, evacuation advisory and  evacuation instruction. In 2021, the law was revised,  Figure 1.   Methodology for the present study . This is because the term “advisories” gave residents a  misperception about the need of evacuation. As a mat- ter of fact, flood evacuation rates in Japan were quite  low. 21  During the flood disaster in the Hiroshima Pre- fecture in 2018, local governments issued evacuation  instructions  to  the  total  number  of  329,203  people.   However, the records of shelter use showed a total of  9,489  people  went  to  145  shelters  in  the  prefecture.   This  indicates  that  the  evacuation  rate  was  as  low   as  2.8  percent.  To  improve  evacuation,  the  use  of   evacuation advisories was abandoned, and evacuation  instruction  is  issued  at  the  time  previously  set  for   evacuation advisories. Since water level is used to issue warnings of dif- ferent  level,  the  key  for  the  system  to  function  prop- erly  is  the  scientific  soundness  of  the  determination   of the evacuation judgment water level and the flood  danger water level. Document analysis also found that at present, all  rivers  in  Japan  are  classified  into  three  categories, 22   namely, rivers with flood forecast, rivers with the pro- vision of water level information, and rivers with flood  alert.  Rivers  with  flood  forecast  are  rivers  flowing   through two or more prefectures or rivers with large  basin  areas  that  are  likely  to  cause  serious  damage   to the national economy if they overflow. Rivers with  the provision of water level information are relatively  small  rivers,  in  which  water  level  may  increase  too   fast  to  predict  with  sufficient  lead  time.  Rivers  with   flood alert are rivers provided with early warning for  mobilizing  flood-fighting  teams  of  local  communities.   This  classification  scheme  and  the  relation  with  the   warning  levels  are  illustrated  in   Table   2.  At  present,   there  are  393  rivers  with  flood  forecast,  1,477  rivers   with  the  provision  of  water  level  information,  and   430  rivers  with  flood  alert. For  the  implementation  of  the  flood  warning   system,  the  criterion  in  determining  water  levels  for   warning is the lead time. The current practice is illus- trated in  Figure  2. For a designated cross-section, we  use  the  water  level  rising  data  to  find  a  water  level   that can provide a 60-minute lead time before it rises  to  the  levee  height.  Then,  we  compared  it  with  the   design  high  water  level  at  the  cross-section,  and  the   lower is chosen as the flood danger water level at the  site. It can also be set as water level corresponding to  flood with a return period of 5~10 years. 23 Evacuation judgment water level is set to provide  a 30-minute lead time before water level rises to flood  danger water level. The rationale is that 30 minutes is  needed  to  open  evacuation  shelters  and  mobilize  the   aged and disabled population. 23 Flood  alert  water  level  can  be  set  as  water  level   when the flow rate is 50 percent of design high water  discharge or water level corresponding to flood with a  return period of 3 years. 23 Chikuma River case In  the  Chikuma  Rive  case,  the  evacuation  judg- ment  water  level  and  flood  dangerous  water  level   at  the  Kuiseke  were  set  to  be  4.6  m  and  5.0  m,   respectively,  as  shown  in   Figure   3a.  On  October  13,   2019,  the  water  level  rising  rate  at  the  evacuation   judgment  water  level  was  0.96  m/h,  and  it  took  25   minutes  for  water  level  to  rise  from  the  evacuation   judgment water level to the flood danger water level.  It  took  another  4  hours  for  the  water  level  to  rise   from the flood danger water level to the levee height.  Therefore,  the  lead  time  provided  by  the  evacuation   judgment  water  level  was  slightly  insufficient,  but   the lead time provided by the flood danger water level  was sufficiently large. On  the  other  hand,  the  two  water  levels  at  the   Tategahana  were  set  to  be  9.1  m  and  9.6  m,  respec- tively,  before  the  disaster.  As  shown  in   Figure   3b,  on   October  13,  2019,  the  water  level  at  the  Tategahana   increased  from  9.1  m  to  9.6  m  in  about  17  minutes,   having  a  water  level  rising  rate  of  1.8  m/h,  and  it   took  more  than  3  hours  for  the  water  level  to  rise   further  to  its  peak. One year after the disaster, the  evacuation judgment water level and the flood danger  water level at the Tategahana were reset to be 7.5 m  and  9.2  m,  respectively,  to  meet  the  requirements  of   lead time. As  far  as  the  Hoyasu  district,  the  worst-affected   area,  was  concerned,  the  lead  time  was  more  than  4   hours with the warning issued according to the water  level at the Kuiseke station because it takes about 4  hours  for  flood  waters  to  travel  from  the  Kuiseke  to   the  Hoyasu.  Analysis  of  documents  of  Nagano  City 24   revealed  that  the  evacuation  advisory  was  issued  to   the  Hoyasu  district  at  6:00   pm ,  October  12  when  the   water level at the Kuise station reached the predeter - mined  evacuation  judgment  water  level.  At  11:40   pm ,  the  evacuation  instruction  was  issued,  which  is  the   Level 4 warning. At 2:00  am , October 13, levee breach  occurred  at  the  Hoyasu  location.  According  to  the   interview conducted after the disaster, several families  evacuated to nearby shelters following the evacuation  advisory and stayed there more than 4 hours. Because  inundation did not happen for a few hours and evacu- ees  did  not  receive  any  update  about  the  flood  from   6:30  pm   to  10:00   pm ,  they  felt  safe  and  returned  to   their homes. As a result, they were stranded by flood  water after the levee breach occurred. This raised two  issues  of  emergency  management.  The  first  is  what   is  the  optimal  lead  time.  Too  short  is  obviously  bad,   but too long may be considered false alarming or not  urgent  and  could  also  be  technically  inaccurate.  The   second is that the lack of information updates inside  evacuation shelters. In a dendritic drainage, the first  issue can be solved by the combination of hydrological  monitoring and channel routing or even simply using  historical data. The examination of major flood hydro- graphs at the two gauging stations during the period  of  2000-2017  found  that  all  major  floods  propagated   from  the  Kuiseke  to  Tategahana  in  6  hours.  Such  a   feature  of  constant  flood  travel  time  can  be  incorpo- rated  in  the  application  of  flood  warning  system  to   different locations in this river reach. It  is  also  worth  mentioning  that  according  to  a   questionnaire  survey  by  Nagano  City, 24   the  evacua- tion rate in this disaster was 54.2 percent, which can  be considered very high in Japan. In our questionnaire survey, 30 replies were obtained  from  foreigners  living  in  the  city,  and  they  were  chosen   randomly  from  streets,  so  that  it  was  a  convenience   sampling. According to their replies, all of them received  flood-related  information  from  friends  and  social  media   in English, and none of them evacuated. In  the  questionnaire  survey,  another  40  replies   were  obtained  from  Japanese  citizens  living  close  to   the  river.  All  of  them  received  warnings  from  author - ity in multiple ways. Nevertheless, a survey targeting  1,826  families  by  the  Chikuma  River  office  showed   that evacuation timing took by residents varied largely,  and  the  majority  started  evacuation  right  after  the   overflow  occurred.  At  that  time,  the  local  fire  brigade   had  been  ringing  the  emergency  bell  for  5  and  a  half   minutes, and actively urged residents to evacuate. 25 Kuma River case The  river  channel  slope  in  the  target  reaches  of   the Kuma River varies from 1/200 to 1/600, while the  channel  slope  in  the  target  reaches  of  the  Chikuma   River  is  between  1/1,000  and  1/1,500.  Therefore,  the   Kuma  River  can  be  considered  a  more  challenging   case for the current warning system in Japan to func- tion as designed. Using   disaster   information   provided   by   MLIT    Kyushu   Regional   Development   Bureau   Yatsushiro    River  and  National  Highway  Office  Japan, 26   Figure   4  shows  the  inundated  areas,  the  fatalities  in  each  area   that occurred in 2020, and the locations of two gauging  stations  in  the  mainstream  of  the  river.  The  evacua- tion  water  level  and  the  flood  danger  water  level  are   3.0  m  and  3.4  m  at  the  Watari  (S1)  station,  while  6.0   m  and  7.6  m  at  the  Hitoyoshi  (S2)  station,  respec- tively.  During  the  flood,  as  shown  in   Figure   5,  it   took  about  40  minutes  for  the  water  to  rise  from  the   evacuation  water  level  to  the  flood  danger  level  and   several  hours  more  to  reach  its  peak.  Therefore,  the   requirements  of  the  multilevel  flood  warning  system   were  satisfied,  and  it  provided  good  lead  time  for     evacuation. The  tragedy  occurred  in  a  nursing   home  for  the  elderly  near  the  river  junction  between   the  Kuma  River  and  a  tributary.  At  10:20   pm ,  July  3,   the  local  village  administration  issued  an  evacuation   advisory,  which  was  a  Level  3  warning.  The  nursing   home  should  start  moving  residents  of  the  nursery   home  to  a  safer  place  following  the  Level  3  warning.   However,  the  evacuation  did  not  take  place  due  to   the  lack  of  staff.  At  that  time,  there  were  70  elderly   but  just  five  staff  in  the  nursing  home. 27   According  to   Kumamoto Daily Newspaper, 28  the local administration  issued  an  evacuation  instruction  at  3:30   am ,  July  4,   which was a Level 4 warning. As one can observe from  Figure   5,  the  flood  danger  water  level  was  reached  at   2:40  am . So, the Level 4 warning was somehow delayed.  Nevertheless,  water  flowed  into  the  nursing  home  at   7:00  am . Therefore, there was sufficient time to complete  evacuation following the evacuation instruction. By the  time  the  danger  became  imminent,  the  staff  tried  to   move all residents to the second floor, but due to limited  time  and  physical  strength,  14  people  in  wheelchairs   were left on the first floor and perished in flooding. In  2017,  Japanese  government  revised  the  Flood   Control Act requiring facilities for the elderly and medi- cal  institutions  in  flood-prone  areas  to  prepare  evacua- tion plans. Following this amendment, the nursing home  in the case prepared an evacuation plan, stipulating the  gathering  of  12  personnel  if  flood  warnings  are  issued   during  night  or  holidays.  Unfortunately,  the  plan  was   not activated properly. However, this inactivity cannot be  simply attributed to the mismanagement of the nursing  home.  Figure  6 shows the locations of the nursing home,  the Watari gauging station (S1), and the location where  the embankment of the tributary was damaged by flood  water  and  a  zoom-in  view  of  the  embankment.  Based   on  newspaper  reports 27-29   and  the  author’s  field  survey,   what happened is reconstructed in timeline as follows: nn At 4:00  am , a staff checked the water level  of the tributary and found that there was  still  some  room  for  flood  water,  so  that  a   decision of wait-and-see was made by the  deputy director of the nursing home. nn Between  5:00  and  6:00   am ,  the  tribu- tary overflowed at the location where the  embankment  height  was  relatively  low   and  damaged  by  flooding,  as  shown  in   Figure  5. nn At  6:00   am ,  because  the  road  in  front  of   the nursing home was inundated, the staff  decided  to  conduct  the  so-called  vertical   evacuation.  However,  there  was  no  eleva- tor  in  the  facility,  and  the  stairway  from   the  first  to  the  second  floor  has  22  steps   and  just  1.2  m  width.  So,  it  is  difficult  to   move a wheelchair to the second floor. nn At  7:00   am ,  flood  water  broke  in  and  the   tragedy occurred. Figure 6. From  these  facts,  it  can  be  concluded  that  the   direct  cause  of  the  tragedy  is  the  overflow  of  the   tributary  and  the  delayed  evacuation  due  partially   to insufficient coping capacity. However, the overflow  might  be  partially  caused  by  the  backwater  effect   of  the  water  level  increase  in  the  mainstream.  This,   indeed, raised a question of how to manage the main- stream  and  tributary  in  an  integrated  manner.  At   present, many small tributaries in Japan do not have  hydrological monitoring stations, impeding integrated  river  basin  management.  In  the  Kuma  River  basin,   there  are  only  four  hydrological  stations  in  tributar - ies, as shown in  Figure  7. As illustrated in  Figure  8, the Kuma River has a  trellis  drainage  pattern.  In  such  a  watershed,  flood   peak  may  occur  at  the  same  time  at  different  loca- tions. Therefore, a well-designed network of hydrolog- ical monitoring stations is critical to issue appropriate  flood  warnings  at  ungaged  sites  because  monitoring   at  one  location  may  not  provide  lead  time  for  down- stream locations. Moreover,  the  delay  of  evacuation  was  also  due   partially  to  road  flooding. 28   This  serves  as  another   evidence  that  better  communication  between  flood   management  sector  and  road  sector  must  be  pro- moted to achieve better flood management. 30 In  this  flood  disaster,  the  Kumamoto  Prefectural   government issued evacuation instructions to 199,044  people  on  July  4,  but  only  1,508  showed  up  in  emer - gency shelters. 31  So, the evacuation rate was as low as  0.75 percent. Such an extremely low rate might imply  the  possibility  of  evacuation,  and  instructions  were   issued  to  more  areas  than  necessary.  In  Hitoyoshi   City and Kuma Village, however, the evacuation rate  was 15.2 and 52.2 percent, respectively. 32 DISCUSSION The flood warning system in Japan was installed  in  2004,  in  which  10  typhoons  made  landfall,  caus- ing  huge  damages.  As  reported  by  Huang, 21   the   evacuation  rates  during  several  major  flood  disas- ters  in  Japan  before  2004  ranged  from  6.1  percent   for  the  Hamada  flood  disaster  to  55.2  percent  for   the  Mobara  flood  disaster.  After  the  implementation   of  flood  warning  system  operation,  the  evacuation   rates  varied  from  21.7  for  the  Oyama  flooding, 33   36   percent  for  the  Sayo  flooding 34   to  67  percent  for  the   Jouso  flooding. 35   However,  in  a  large  flood  disaster   affecting  seven  cities  in  Western  Japan  in  2018,  the   evacuation  rate  was  1.9  percent  in  Gero  City  and   46  percent  in  Saka  Town,  having  an  average  rate  of   11  percent. 36,37   These  data  indicated  that  there  is  no   Figure  7. On  the  other  hand,  from  the   data  after  2004,  this  study  found  that  a  relationship   may exist between population and evacuation rate for  cities with a population less than 40,000, as shown in  Figure   9.  The  smaller  the  population,  the  higher  the   evacuation rate. This can be explained by the fact that  community  strength  is  strong  in  small  cities  due  to   the  easiness  of  networking,  which  can  help  informa- tion dissemination greatly and provide evacuation aid  to those in need as well. Thus, it may be hypothesized  that  such  a  relationship  might  have  been  existing   before  2004.  However,  it  cannot  be  validated  at  this   moment due to data insufficiency. In 2017, Flood Control Act of Japan was amended,  demanding zero evacuation delay. To achieve this goal,  the  amendment  stipulates  for  the  establishment  of   Council for Large-Scale Flood Mitigation in all target  regions by 2021. Although the requirement for council  set up was achieved in 2021, this study found that the  first meeting of the Council for the Kuma River basin  was  held  on  October  27,  2020,  more  than  2  months   after  the  disaster.  In  Nagano  Prefecture,  Council  for   Large-Scale Flood Mitigation was established in 2017  and  has  held  annual  meetings  to  discuss  various   measures  so  far.  This  may  partially  explain  why  the   evacuation rate in the Chikuma River case was much  high than that in the Kuma River case. Based on above-mentioned findings, a SWOT anal- ysis  was  conducted.  SWOT  analysis  is  a  structured   planning method that evaluates those four elements of  an  organization,  project  or  business  venture.  Because   it  is  a  simple,  but  powerful  framework  for  leveraging   the  organization’s  strengths,  improving  weaknesses,   minimizing  threats,  and  taking  the  greatest  possible   advantage of opportunities, this study employed SWOT  analysis  to  discuss  how  to  move  forward  with  the  cur - rent  flood  warning  system  in  Japan.   Figure   10  shows   the pros and cons of the current flood warning system  in Japan, and the cross analysis is given as follows: Leverage  (strengths  +  opportunities):  As  a  law   amendment  demands  100  percent  evacuation  rate,   expansion  and  refinement  of  the  flood  warning  sys- tem will be further promoted. Inhibitory  (weaknesses  +  opportunities):  If  the   awareness  of  the  public  about  flood  risk  is  not   increased and evacuation warnings are not obeyed by  residents, all commitments by local authorities would  end up in vain. Vulnerability   (strengths   +   threats):   Climate    change  may  change  flood  dynamics,  so  that  the  lead   times  provided  by  the  current  system  might  become   insufficient in the near future. It is not only just due  to  the  shortening  of  flood  peak  arrival  time  but  also   because physical aging may require more time to pre- pare  for  evacuation.  On  the  other  hand,  an  unneces- sary large lead time may negatively affect evacuation,  especially in an aging society due to cognitive aging. Problematic  (weaknesses  +  threats):  As  senior   people stay in rural areas and young people move to  large  cities,  the  unavailability  of  sufficient  human   resources  for  emergence  response  in  rural  areas  will   impede the realization of zero evacuation delay. Following the cross analysis, a new framework for  improving  the  effectiveness  of  flood  warning  system   in  mobilizing  evacuation  is  presented  in   Figure   11.  It has three dimensions. An effective warning system  should  have  the  right  number  of  automatic  hydro- logical  stations  at  the  right  places  along  both  the   mainstream  and  tributaries  of  a  river.  More  gener - ally,  advanced  technical  capacity  development  is   required,  which  allows  real  time  data  collection  and   transmission  and  timely  analysis  for  warning  issu- ance. On the other hand, optimal lead times should be  designed  for  residential  communities  in  flood-prone   areas  based  on  channel  routing  with  consideration   of  human  perception  and  behavior. However, the longer the lead time,  the greater the degree of uncertainty in the flood fore- cast and human behavior. Too large a lead time might  lower  alert  level  of  residents.  Such  a  psychological   factor has been poorly considered in evacuation plan- ning so far. According  to  the  John  Leach’s  disaster  psychol- ogy  theory,  there  are  three  phases  in  human  behav- ior  in  relation  to  disasters:  before,  during,  and  after   the  impact  of  disaster.  Before  the  impact,  people  are   aware of the coming impact but try to ignore or deny  the  facts,  reducing  uneasy  feelings  of  danger  and   showing  apathetic  behavior  with  respect  to  the  real   danger.  Therefore,  a  large  lead  time  could  become   an excuse for residents not to act quickly or take the  wrong  action  as  revealed  in  the  study.  It  is  hypoth- esized here that the relationship between evacuation  rate and lead time takes an inverse U-shape. As lead  time  increases,  evacuation  rate  will  increase  at  first   and then decrease once the lead time reaches its turn- ing point. This turning point is the optimal lead time,  and its determination is critical for better emergency  management. Furthermore,  evacuation-aiding  capacity  should   be  built  up  together  with  flood  forecasting  capacity.   A flood warning system without emergency response  capacity  will  not  function  effectively,  no  matter  how   accurate and reliable the warning system is. A funda- mental  issue  is  that  disaster  resilience  is  frequently   pursued  separately  by  the  public  and  private  sec- tors. Building public–private partnerships to enhance  emergency capacity is a key for disaster reduction.
